postings.conferenceName: 7th International Conference on Natural Language Computing Advances (NLCA 2026)
postings.conferenceText: 7th International Conference on Natural Language Computing Advances (NLCA 2026)October 24 ~ 25, 2026, Vienna, Austriahttps://cbiot2026.org/nlca/indexScope7th International Conference on Natural Language Computing Advances (NLCA 2026) provides a premier global forum for presenting and exchanging cutting edge research, theoretical insights, advanced methodologies and impactful applications across the rapidly evolving field of Natural Language Processing. As language technologies continue to transform scientific discovery, industry innovation and human–computer interaction, NLCA 2026 brings together leading researchers, practitioners and technologists to share breakthroughs, discuss emerging challenges and explore the future of intelligent language systems.NLCA 2026 welcomes substantial contributions in both foundational and frontier areas of NLP, including large language models, LLM reasoning and tool use, retrieval augmented generation, multimodal NLP, dialogue systems and LLM agents, machine translation and multilingual NLP, information extraction, semantic processing, speech and audio language models, efficient NLP, continual and streaming NLP, scientific NLP and responsible, explainable and secure NLP. The conference also embraces emerging domains such as synthetic data generation, dataset governance, LLM safety, hallucination mitigation, language conditioned robotics and NLP for misinformation and societal impact.Authors are invited to submit high quality articles presenting research results, experimental studies, survey papers, industrial experiences and novel applications that highlight significant progress in Natural Language Processing and its rapidly expanding ecosystem of intelligent language technologies.Topics of interest include, but are not limited to, the following Large Language Models and Foundation Models LLM Reasoning, Planning and Tool Use Instruction Tuning, Alignment and RLHF Prompt Engineering and In Context Learning Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and Long Context Retrieval Neural Search, Vector Databases and LLM Enhanced Ranking Multimodal NLP (Vision Language, Audio Language, Video Language) Embodied NLP and Language Conditioned Robotics Dialogue Systems, Conversational AI and LLM Agents Machine Translation, Multilingual NLP and Cultural Adaptation Information Extraction, Text Mining and Knowledge Graphs Semantic Processing, NLI and Paraphrase/Entailment Synthetic Data Generation and Auto Labeling Efficient NLP: LoRA, MoE, Distillation and Edge Optimized LLMs Continual, Streaming and Adaptive NLP Speech Recognition, Synthesis and Audio LLMs NLP for Healthcare, Finance, Legal and Scientific Discovery NLP for Social Media, Misinformation and Digital Humanities Explainable NLP, Bias/Fairness and Ethical AI Robust NLP, Adversarial Attacks and Hallucination Mitigation Privacy Preserving NLP and Federated Learning LLM Benchmarking, Evaluation and Human in the Loop TestingPaper SubmissionAuthors are invited to submit papers through the conference Submission System by September 26, 2026. Submissions must be original and should not have been published previously or be under consideration for publication while being evaluated for this conference. The proceedings of the conference will be published by Computer Science Conference Proceedings in Computer Science & Information Technology (CS & IT) series (Confirmed).Selected papers from NLCA 2026, after further revisions, will be published in the special issue of the following journal. International Journal on Natural Language Computing (IJNLC) International Journal on Information Theory (IJIT) International Journal on Computational Science & Applications (IJCSA) Machine Learning and Applications: An International Journal (MLAIJ) International Journal of Web & Semantic Technology (IJWesT)Important Dates Submission Deadline: September 26, 2026 Authors Notification: October 10, 2026 Registration & camera - Ready Paper Due: October 17, 2026Contact UsHere's where you can reach us: nlca@cbiot2026.org (or) nlcaconfe@gmail.com

postings.conferenceName: ISTANBUL 5th International Conference on Agricultural Technology & Food Security (IATFS-27) scheduled on Dec. 16-17, 2027 Istanbul (Türkiye)
postings.conferenceText: TopicsAll Abstracts, Reviews, short articles, Full articles, Posters are welcomed related with any of the following research fields:Agricultural Technology & Food Security1. Precision AgriculturePrecision agriculture focuses on using digital technologies to manage farms more accurately and efficiently. It includes GPS-guided tractors, field mapping, variable-rate application of fertilizers and pesticides, soil sensing, crop monitoring, yield mapping, satellite imagery, drones, and data-driven decision-making. It can improve productivity while reducing unnecessary use of water, chemicals, fuel, and other resources.2. Smart Farming and the Internet of ThingsSmart farming uses connected devices and sensors to continuously monitor agricultural conditions. Important areas include soil-moisture sensors, temperature and humidity monitoring, weather stations, livestock tracking devices, automated irrigation, greenhouse monitoring, remote farm-control systems, wireless sensor networks, cloud platforms, and real-time farm alerts.3. Artificial Intelligence in AgricultureArtificial intelligence can help farmers recognize patterns, predict problems, and automate decisions. Relevant areas include crop-disease detection, weed identification, pest recognition, yield prediction, weather-based recommendations, automated harvesting, image analysis, farm-management assistants, predictive maintenance of machinery, and AI-based irrigation or fertilizer scheduling.4. Agricultural Robotics and AutomationRobotics can reduce repetitive manual work and improve farming precision. This area includes autonomous tractors, robotic harvesters, fruit-picking robots, robotic weed removal, automated seed planting, agricultural drones, livestock-feeding robots, robotic milking systems, sorting robots, packing systems, and autonomous field vehicles.5. Agricultural DronesDrones are increasingly used for monitoring and managing farmland. Applications include crop-health imaging, field surveying, plant counting, fertilizer spraying, pesticide application, irrigation inspection, pest detection, livestock monitoring, thermal imaging, mapping damaged crops, and assessing farms after floods, storms, or droughts.6. Remote Sensing and Satellite AgricultureSatellite and aerial information can support large-scale agricultural monitoring. Important areas include vegetation indices, crop-health assessment, drought monitoring, soil-moisture estimation, land-use mapping, crop-area estimation, weather observation, yield forecasting, irrigation monitoring, and early identification of crop stress.7. Soil Technology and Soil HealthHealthy soil is essential for long-term food production. Key areas include soil sensors, soil testing, nutrient monitoring, soil-moisture measurement, soil-carbon assessment, erosion prevention, organic matter management, conservation tillage, crop rotation, soil restoration, microbial activity, and technologies for preventing soil degradation.8. Smart Irrigation and Water ManagementAgriculture is one of the largest users of freshwater, making efficient irrigation important for food security. Areas include drip irrigation, sensor-controlled irrigation, automated irrigation scheduling, rainwater harvesting, groundwater monitoring, wastewater reuse, irrigation forecasting, desalination for agriculture, water-loss detection, and drought-resistant farming systems.9. Agricultural BiotechnologyBiotechnology can help improve productivity, crop quality, and resistance to environmental pressures. Important areas include genetically modified crops, gene editing, CRISPR applications, disease-resistant plants, drought-resistant crops, salt-tolerant crops, biofortification, tissue culture, plant breeding, microbial fertilizers, and biological pest-control products.10. Seed Technology and Crop ImprovementBetter seeds can increase production and reduce vulnerability to climate and disease. This includes hybrid seeds, improved crop varieties, seed preservation, seed treatment, high-yield varieties, early-maturing crops, climate-resilient seeds, disease-resistant varieties, seed banks, genetic diversity, and indigenous crop varieties.11. Climate-Smart AgricultureClimate-smart agriculture aims to maintain food production while adapting to climate change. Relevant areas include climate-resilient crops, drought adaptation, flood-resistant agriculture, carbon-efficient farming, agroforestry, conservation agriculture, water-efficient production, renewable-powered farms, climate forecasting, and agricultural risk management.12. Climate Change and Food SecurityChanges in temperature, rainfall, drought frequency, floods, storms, and sea levels can affect food production. Important areas include crop-yield losses, changing growing seasons, livestock heat stress, water shortages, soil degradation, new pests and diseases, fisheries disruption, food-price volatility, agricultural adaptation, and resilience planning.13. Vertical FarmingVertical farming produces crops in stacked indoor environments and can reduce dependence on large areas of farmland. Relevant areas include controlled-environment agriculture, LED lighting, automated nutrient delivery, climate control, vertical growing systems, urban farming, energy consumption, water recycling, crop selection, and economic feasibility.14. HydroponicsHydroponics grows plants without conventional soil by supplying nutrients through water. Important areas include nutrient solutions, water recirculation, greenhouse hydroponics, nutrient-film technique, deep-water culture, drip hydroponics, automation, pH monitoring, electrical-conductivity monitoring, urban food production, and water efficiency.15. AquaponicsAquaponics combines fish production with hydroponic plant cultivation. Fish waste provides nutrients for plants, while plants help clean the water. Relevant areas include fish farming, water recycling, nutrient circulation, biological filtration, plant production, controlled environments, sustainable protein production, system monitoring, and urban agriculture.16. AeroponicsAeroponics grows plants with roots suspended in air and supplied with nutrient mist. It relates to high-efficiency water use, indoor agriculture, root-zone monitoring, nutrient management, controlled environments, vertical farms, space-efficient agriculture, propagation systems, and automated misting technologies.17. Greenhouse TechnologyGreenhouses allow crops to grow under controlled conditions. Areas include temperature regulation, ventilation, humidity control, automated irrigation, artificial lighting, carbon-dioxide management, pest protection, intelligent climate systems, greenhouse sensors, energy-efficient design, and year-round crop production.18. Controlled-Environment AgricultureControlled-environment agriculture uses technology to regulate plant-growing conditions. It includes smart greenhouses, indoor farms, climate-controlled chambers, lighting management, air circulation, nutrient monitoring, carbon-dioxide control, water recycling, automation, and digital environmental management.19. Agricultural MachineryMechanization improves productivity and reduces heavy manual labour. Relevant areas include tractors, combine harvesters, seed drills, cultivators, sprayers, irrigation pumps, threshers, tillage machines, autonomous machinery, electric farm vehicles, equipment maintenance, and energy-efficient machinery.20. Electrification of AgricultureElectric technologies are increasingly replacing diesel-powered agricultural equipment. This includes electric tractors, battery-powered machinery, electric irrigation pumps, solar-powered equipment, farm charging infrastructure, energy storage, microgrids, electrified greenhouses, and renewable-energy integration.21. Renewable Energy in AgricultureRenewable energy can reduce operating costs and dependence on fossil fuels. Important applications include solar irrigation pumps, solar-powered greenhouses, wind-powered farms, agricultural biogas, biomass energy, farm microgrids, battery storage, agrivoltaics, and renewable-powered refrigeration.22. AgrivoltaicsAgrivoltaics combines solar-energy generation with agricultural production on the same land. Relevant areas include solar panels above crops, crop shading, water conservation, farm electricity production, land-use efficiency, livestock grazing beneath solar installations, microclimate effects, and economic viability.23. Agricultural Waste ManagementAgricultural production generates crop residues, animal waste, wastewater, plastics, and food-processing waste. Important areas include composting, anaerobic digestion, manure treatment, biomass conversion, recycling agricultural plastics, biochar production, waste-to-energy systems, nutrient recovery, and circular agriculture.24. Circular AgricultureCircular agriculture aims to reuse resources instead of treating them as waste. It includes recycling nutrients, converting manure into fertilizer, using crop residues for energy, wastewater reuse, food-waste recovery, compost production, insect-based recycling, industrial symbiosis, and closed-loop production systems.25. Sustainable AgricultureSustainable agriculture seeks to maintain productivity while protecting natural resources. Areas include reduced pesticide use, organic farming, conservation agriculture, crop rotation, integrated farming, biodiversity protection, efficient irrigation, sustainable fertilizer use, soil conservation, renewable energy, and reduced greenhouse-gas emissions.26. Regenerative AgricultureRegenerative agriculture emphasizes restoring soil and ecosystems. It includes cover crops, reduced tillage, crop rotation, rotational grazing, compost application, agroforestry, carbon sequestration, biodiversity enhancement, soil-microbe management, and restoration of degraded farmland.27. Organic FarmingOrganic farming minimizes synthetic chemicals and emphasizes natural biological processes. Important areas include organic fertilizers, biological pest control, crop rotation, composting, certification standards, organic seeds, natural weed management, soil fertility, consumer demand, and organic food supply chains.28. Integrated Pest ManagementIntegrated pest management combines different methods to control pests while reducing chemical pesticide use. It includes biological control, pest monitoring, resistant crops, crop rotation, pheromone traps, targeted spraying, beneficial insects, forecasting systems, digital pest detection, and farmer education.29. Plant Disease ManagementPlant diseases can significantly reduce food production. Relevant areas include early disease detection, resistant crops, biological control, fungicide management, remote sensing, AI-based diagnosis, pathogen monitoring, quarantine measures, disease forecasting, and clean seed programs.30. Fertilizer TechnologyModern fertilizer technologies aim to provide crops with nutrients more efficiently. Areas include precision fertilization, controlled-release fertilizers, nano-fertilizers, biofertilizers, nitrogen-use efficiency, phosphorus recovery, soil nutrient mapping, fertigation, organic fertilizers, and environmental impacts of fertilizer overuse.31. BiofertilizersBiofertilizers use beneficial microorganisms to improve plant nutrition. Relevant areas include nitrogen-fixing bacteria, phosphate-solubilizing microorganisms, mycorrhizal fungi, microbial soil treatments, biological nitrogen fixation, reduced chemical fertilizer dependence, and sustainable soil fertility.32. Biological Pest ControlBiological pest control uses natural enemies and biological agents rather than relying solely on synthetic pesticides. It includes beneficial insects, predatory organisms, microbial pesticides, fungi, bacteria, parasitoids, pheromone systems, and habitat management.33. Livestock TechnologyTechnology can improve animal health, productivity, and welfare. Relevant areas include wearable livestock sensors, GPS tracking, automated feeding, robotic milking, disease detection, reproductive monitoring, smart barns, livestock identification, weight monitoring, and precision livestock farming.34. Precision Livestock FarmingPrecision livestock farming uses sensors and automation to monitor individual animals. It includes activity trackers, health monitoring, automated feeding, milk-production monitoring, body-temperature sensors, behaviour analysis, reproductive monitoring, computer vision, and AI-based disease detection.35. Aquaculture TechnologyAquaculture can provide fish and seafood while reducing pressure on wild fisheries. Important areas include automated feeding, water-quality sensors, recirculating aquaculture systems, disease monitoring, fish-growth tracking, oxygen management, offshore aquaculture, sustainable fish feed, and smart aquaculture farms.36. Fisheries TechnologyTechnology can support sustainable management of marine food resources. Relevant areas include GPS fishing systems, sonar, electronic monitoring, vessel tracking, fish-stock assessment, satellite observation, sustainable fishing equipment, illegal-fishing detection, seafood traceability, and ecosystem monitoring.37. Alternative ProteinsAlternative proteins can reduce pressure on land, water, and conventional livestock systems. This area includes plant-based proteins, cultivated meat, fermentation-derived proteins, insect protein, algae-based food, microbial protein, consumer acceptance, food safety, nutritional quality, and production costs.38. Cultivated MeatCultivated meat is produced from animal cells without raising and slaughtering whole animals. Important areas include cell culture, bioreactors, growth media, tissue engineering, scaling production, food safety, environmental impacts, regulation, consumer acceptance, and commercial viability.39. Insect FarmingInsects can be used as food, livestock feed, and a method of converting organic waste into useful protein. Relevant areas include mealworms, crickets, black soldier flies, feed production, food-waste recycling, protein efficiency, animal nutrition, processing technologies, safety, and consumer acceptance.40. Food Processing TechnologyFood processing technologies help preserve food, improve safety, and extend shelf life. Areas include pasteurization, freezing, drying, fermentation, thermal processing, high-pressure processing, irradiation, aseptic processing, automation, quality control, and nutrient preservation.41. Food PreservationReducing spoilage is central to food security. Relevant methods include refrigeration, freezing, drying, canning, fermentation, vacuum packaging, modified-atmosphere packaging, preservatives, cold plasma, irradiation, and intelligent storage systems.42. Cold-Chain TechnologyCold chains protect perishable food from production to consumption. Important areas include refrigerated transport, cold warehouses, temperature sensors, smart packaging, real-time tracking, backup power, vaccine-style monitoring technologies for food, energy-efficient cooling, and rural cold-storage systems.43. Food Storage TechnologyImproved storage reduces post-harvest losses. This includes grain silos, hermetic storage, temperature-controlled warehouses, humidity monitoring, pest-resistant storage, automated inventories, refrigerated storage, modified atmospheres, rural storage facilities, and intelligent warehouse systems.44. Post-Harvest TechnologyLarge quantities of food can be lost after harvesting. Relevant areas include mechanical harvesting, drying, cleaning, grading, sorting, packaging, transportation, storage, cold chains, quality monitoring, and technologies for reducing damage and spoilage.45. Food Packaging TechnologyPackaging protects food from contamination and deterioration. Important areas include biodegradable packaging, active packaging, intelligent packaging, antimicrobial films, modified-atmosphere packaging, freshness indicators, temperature indicators, recyclable materials, edible packaging, and packaging-waste reduction.46. Food Waste ReductionFood waste affects both sustainability and food availability. Key areas include waste monitoring, improved storage, intelligent expiration labels, food redistribution platforms, better supply forecasting, consumer education, processing imperfect produce, composting, food donation, and waste-to-energy technologies.47. Food Supply-Chain ManagementFood security depends on reliable movement of food from farms to consumers. Relevant areas include transportation, logistics, storage, distribution centres, inventory control, supply forecasting, digital tracking, cold chains, risk management, and emergency food-distribution networks.48. Blockchain in AgricultureBlockchain can improve transparency and traceability in agricultural supply chains. Applications include tracing food origin, verifying organic products, recording farm transactions, monitoring supply chains, smart contracts, certification verification, food-safety investigations, and reducing fraud.49. Food TraceabilityTraceability systems help identify where food comes from and where it travels. This includes QR codes, RFID, blockchain, digital farm records, batch tracking, livestock identification, warehouse records, contamination tracing, certification systems, and consumer transparency.50. Big Data in AgricultureAgricultural data can be collected from machinery, satellites, sensors, markets, weather systems, and farms. Important areas include data analytics, farm databases, predictive models, yield optimization, risk forecasting, machine-learning models, decision-support systems, data ownership, and agricultural data platforms.51. Farm Management Information SystemsDigital management platforms help farmers organize production and business decisions. They can include crop planning, machinery records, fertilizer use, irrigation scheduling, livestock records, financial management, inventory management, weather information, compliance records, and yield analysis.52. Digital Agriculture PlatformsDigital platforms connect farmers with information and services. Areas include mobile agricultural applications, weather information, market prices, crop advice, digital marketplaces, insurance platforms, agricultural financing, remote advisory services, and farmer-to-consumer platforms.53. Agricultural Mobile ApplicationsMobile technology can provide farmers with low-cost access to useful information. Applications include weather alerts, pest identification, crop calendars, fertilizer recommendations, irrigation advice, market-price information, veterinary services, agricultural training, and digital payments.54. Digital Agricultural ExtensionTraditional agricultural advisory services can be expanded through digital systems. Relevant approaches include mobile advice, online training, AI agricultural assistants, farmer helplines, video education, digital demonstration farms, remote diagnosis, and localized agricultural information.55. Agricultural CybersecurityAs farms become connected, they can become vulnerable to cyber threats. Important areas include protecting smart tractors, irrigation systems, agricultural databases, IoT sensors, farm-management software, autonomous machines, supply-chain platforms, and food-processing infrastructure.56. Agricultural Data PrivacyDigital agriculture creates questions about who owns and controls farm data. Relevant issues include farmer privacy, machinery-generated data, cloud storage, third-party access, data sharing, cybersecurity, agricultural platform agreements, and regulatory frameworks.57. Rural ConnectivityModern agricultural technology depends on reliable internet and telecommunications. Relevant areas include rural broadband, 5G agriculture, satellite internet, low-power wide-area networks, LoRaWAN, wireless sensor networks, edge computing, and affordable digital infrastructure.58. 5G and Future Communications in AgricultureAdvanced communications can support autonomous equipment and real-time agricultural monitoring. Applications include connected tractors, drones, robot coordination, high-resolution farm cameras, livestock tracking, remote machinery control, edge computing, and smart agricultural facilities.59. Weather Technology for AgricultureReliable weather information helps farmers make better decisions. Areas include weather stations, satellite forecasting, rainfall prediction, frost warnings, drought forecasting, heatwave alerts, storm monitoring, microclimate sensors, and AI-based agricultural weather models.60. Agricultural Early-Warning SystemsEarly-warning technologies can reduce losses from climate events, pests, and diseases. This includes drought alerts, flood warnings, pest outbreaks, crop-disease forecasting, heat stress warnings, food-price alerts, livestock-disease surveillance, and emergency agricultural planning.61. Crop Yield ForecastingAccurate yield forecasts can improve food planning. Methods include satellite imaging, weather data, AI models, soil information, historical yields, crop-growth models, drone imagery, and regional production databases.62. Food Security MonitoringFood security monitoring helps governments and organizations detect areas at risk of hunger. Important indicators include food availability, food affordability, agricultural production, nutrition levels, market prices, household income, climate conditions, conflict risks, and emergency food requirements.63. The Four Dimensions of Food SecurityFood security is commonly examined through food availability, access, utilization, and stability. Technology can influence each dimension through higher agricultural productivity, better transport, reduced food losses, improved nutrition, price monitoring, and resilient food systems.64. Food AvailabilityFood availability concerns whether sufficient food is produced or supplied. Relevant issues include crop production, livestock production, fisheries, imports, agricultural productivity, storage capacity, food reserves, and production technologies.65. Food AccessFood access concerns whether people can physically and economically obtain food. Important factors include income, food prices, transport, market infrastructure, social protection, rural roads, agricultural employment, and digital food marketplaces.66. Food Utilization and NutritionFood security also depends on whether food provides adequate nutrition. Relevant areas include dietary diversity, food safety, clean water, sanitation, micronutrient deficiencies, fortified foods, biofortified crops, nutrition education, and food quality.67. Food-System StabilityStable food systems must continue functioning despite shocks. Relevant risks include droughts, floods, war, pandemics, energy shortages, supply-chain disruption, crop failures, economic crises, and food-price spikes.68. Nutrition SecurityNutrition security goes beyond simply having enough calories. Important areas include protein availability, micronutrients, vitamins, minerals, childhood nutrition, maternal nutrition, fortified foods, biofortification, dietary diversity, and affordable healthy diets.69. BiofortificationBiofortification improves the nutritional content of crops through breeding or biotechnology. Examples include vitamin-A-rich crops, iron-rich crops, zinc-enhanced grains, and nutrient-dense staple foods designed to reduce micronutrient deficiencies.70. Food Fortification TechnologyFood fortification adds nutrients during processing. Areas include fortified flour, iodine-enriched salt, vitamin-fortified foods, mineral supplementation, quality control, public-health programs, food standards, and distribution to vulnerable populations.71. Food Safety TechnologyTechnology can reduce contamination and foodborne illness. Important areas include biosensors, rapid pathogen detection, automated inspections, food-quality sensors, contamination monitoring, cold-chain control, traceability systems, laboratory testing, and intelligent packaging.72. Biosensors in Agriculture and FoodBiosensors can rapidly detect biological or chemical conditions. Applications include soil nutrient monitoring, plant-disease detection, pesticide residue detection, pathogen detection, milk-quality testing, meat-quality assessment, water contamination, and food freshness monitoring.73. Nanotechnology in AgricultureNanotechnology has applications in fertilizers, pesticides, sensors, packaging, and food preservation. Areas include nano-fertilizers, nano-pesticides, nanosensors, smart delivery systems, antimicrobial packaging, water treatment, plant nutrition, and environmental safety.74. Food Quality ControlMaintaining consistent food quality involves physical, chemical, biological, and digital monitoring. Relevant areas include machine vision, automated sorting, laboratory testing, spectroscopy, sensors, contamination detection, grading systems, and quality certification.75. Agricultural Market TechnologyDigital markets can connect producers directly with buyers. Relevant areas include electronic marketplaces, commodity-price platforms, online auctions, farmer cooperatives, direct-to-consumer sales, digital payments, logistics platforms, and transparent pricing.76. Digital Payments and Agricultural FinanceFinancial technology can help farmers access markets and investment. Important areas include mobile payments, digital banking, agricultural loans, microfinance, farm credit scoring, crowdfunding, digital insurance, and financial inclusion for rural communities.77. Agricultural Insurance TechnologyFarmers face risks from weather, disease, and market fluctuations. Technologies include satellite-based crop insurance, weather-index insurance, automated claims, remote damage assessment, drone-based assessment, digital policies, and climate-risk modelling.78. Food Price MonitoringDigital systems can track agricultural and food prices in real time. Relevant areas include market databases, mobile price alerts, commodity exchanges, inflation monitoring, early-warning systems, price forecasting, and detecting supply shortages.79. Agricultural Economics and Technology AdoptionNew agricultural technologies depend on economic viability. Important issues include equipment costs, return on investment, access to finance, farm size, labour savings, productivity gains, technology acceptance, rural infrastructure, and government support.80. Smallholder Farmers and TechnologySmall farms produce a significant share of food in many regions. Relevant areas include affordable farm machinery, low-cost sensors, mobile agricultural services, micro-irrigation, cooperative ownership, digital financing, market access, training, and locally appropriate technologies.81. Women in Agriculture and TechnologyTechnology can improve productivity and opportunities for women farmers. Important areas include access to machinery, digital financial services, mobile agricultural information, land rights, training, entrepreneurship, labour-saving technologies, and participation in agricultural value chains.82. Youth and Agricultural InnovationTechnology can make agriculture more attractive to younger generations. Relevant areas include agritech startups, digital farming, drones, robotics, agricultural entrepreneurship, online marketplaces, agricultural education, innovation hubs, and rural employment.83. Agricultural Education and TrainingSuccessful adoption of agricultural technologies requires skilled users. Areas include vocational training, university agricultural engineering, digital literacy, extension programs, farmer field schools, equipment training, online courses, and technology demonstration centres.84. Agritech StartupsAgricultural startups develop new technologies for farming and food systems. Areas include robotics, farm software, sensors, biotechnology, food technology, vertical farming, alternative proteins, agricultural marketplaces, supply-chain technology, and agricultural finance.85. Agricultural Research and InnovationResearch institutions play an important role in developing future food technologies. Relevant areas include crop genetics, farm machinery, robotics, soil science, irrigation research, livestock science, food engineering, biotechnology, climate modelling, and field experimentation.86. Smart VillagesSmart-village concepts apply digital infrastructure to rural development. Relevant areas include renewable energy, rural broadband, smart agriculture, digital healthcare, e-learning, local food processing, water management, digital government services, and rural entrepreneurship.87. Urban AgricultureUrban agriculture can produce food closer to consumers. It includes rooftop gardens, community gardens, vertical farms, indoor farms, hydroponics, aquaponics, greenhouse farming, urban composting, local food networks, and building-integrated agriculture.88. Peri-Urban AgricultureAgriculture around cities can provide fresh food while connecting rural production with urban markets. Relevant areas include vegetable farming, dairy production, greenhouse agriculture, local distribution, urban food planning, waste recycling, and short food-supply chains.89. Local Food SystemsLocal food systems reduce the distance between producers and consumers. Areas include farmers' markets, farm-to-school programs, direct sales, community-supported agriculture, food cooperatives, urban agriculture, local processing, and regional food networks.90. Food Miles and Sustainable DistributionReducing unnecessary transport can lower environmental impacts. Relevant areas include local sourcing, transportation efficiency, distribution-centre optimization, electric delivery vehicles, refrigerated logistics, route optimization, and regional food production.91. Agricultural TransportationReliable transportation is essential for reducing food losses and improving market access. Areas include rural roads, refrigerated vehicles, autonomous transport, electric trucks, logistics optimization, GPS tracking, rail transport, and last-mile food delivery.92. Smart WarehousingSmart warehouses can improve agricultural storage and distribution. Technologies include automated inventory systems, robots, RFID tags, temperature sensors, humidity control, AI demand forecasting, warehouse-management software, and automated sorting.93. Agricultural LogisticsAgricultural logistics links farms, processors, warehouses, retailers, and consumers. Important areas include route planning, fleet management, cold chains, inventory systems, distribution networks, food traceability, transportation costs, and digital logistics platforms.94. Resilient Food Supply ChainsResilient supply chains can continue operating during emergencies. Relevant areas include diversified suppliers, strategic reserves, local food production, alternative transport routes, predictive analytics, emergency warehouses, flexible processing capacity, and digital supply-chain visibility.95. Food Reserves and Strategic StorageGovernments may maintain food reserves to manage emergencies and price shocks. Relevant issues include grain storage, reserve management, warehouse technology, spoilage prevention, stock rotation, emergency distribution, and national food-security planning.96. Emergency AgricultureAgricultural systems often need support after wars, floods, droughts, earthquakes, or other disasters. Relevant areas include emergency seeds, temporary irrigation, mobile agricultural equipment, rapid livestock support, emergency food production, agricultural recovery, and humanitarian logistics.97. Conflict and Food SecurityConflict can damage agricultural production and disrupt food supplies. Important areas include damaged farmland, labour shortages, transport disruptions, blocked trade routes, energy shortages, food-price increases, refugee food security, agricultural reconstruction, and humanitarian assistance.98. Geopolitics of FoodFood systems are affected by international trade and political relationships. Relevant areas include grain exports, fertilizer supply, energy prices, trade restrictions, agricultural sanctions, strategic commodities, import dependence, national self-sufficiency, and international food agreements.99. Food Trade and Global Food SecurityInternational trade can help balance food shortages between regions. Important areas include food imports and exports, tariffs, trade agreements, global grain markets, supply-chain dependency, shipping routes, export bans, food-price transmission, and trade diversification.100. National Food Self-SufficiencyCountries may seek to produce a larger share of their own food. Relevant areas include domestic agricultural capacity, strategic crops, protected agriculture, irrigation expansion, food reserves, agricultural subsidies, technological modernization, and import dependence.101. Food SovereigntyFood sovereignty concerns the ability of communities and nations to shape their own food systems. Areas include local production, smallholder agriculture, indigenous farming knowledge, land access, seed ownership, sustainable agriculture, local markets, and community participation.102. Land ManagementEffective land management is necessary for sustainable food production. Relevant areas include agricultural zoning, land-use planning, preventing farmland loss, soil conservation, land restoration, satellite mapping, land registration, and sustainable intensification.103. Land DegradationLand degradation reduces agricultural productivity. Important causes and responses include erosion, salinization, desertification, nutrient depletion, deforestation, overgrazing, soil compaction, restoration technologies, reforestation, and conservation agriculture.104. Desertification and AgricultureDesertification threatens food production in dry regions. Relevant areas include drought-resistant crops, water harvesting, soil conservation, windbreaks, agroforestry, controlled grazing, irrigation efficiency, land restoration, and dryland farming technologies.105. AgroforestryAgroforestry combines trees with crops or livestock. Important areas include soil protection, carbon storage, biodiversity, shade management, water conservation, wind protection, fruit and timber production, livestock integration, and climate resilience.106. Biodiversity and Food SecurityAgricultural biodiversity can make food systems more resilient. Relevant areas include crop diversity, genetic diversity, pollinators, soil organisms, traditional crop varieties, wild relatives of crops, habitat conservation, and reduced monoculture dependence.107. Pollination Technology and Pollinator ProtectionMany food crops depend on pollinating insects. Areas include bee monitoring, smart beehives, pollinator habitats, pesticide management, robotic pollination, drone pollination research, ecosystem restoration, and pollination-service management.108. Water Security and Food SecurityWater availability is directly connected with agricultural production. Important areas include irrigation efficiency, groundwater depletion, rainfall variability, water storage, water recycling, watershed management, desalination, drought planning, and competition for water resources.109. Energy Security and Food SecurityFood production depends on energy for machinery, fertilizer manufacturing, irrigation, refrigeration, processing, and transport. Relevant areas include fuel prices, electricity availability, renewable energy, energy-efficient farming, fertilizer production, and energy-independent farms.110. Water-Energy-Food NexusWater, energy, and food systems are strongly interconnected. Examples include energy needed for irrigation, water needed for energy production, energy required for food processing, agricultural biomass for energy, and competition between resources.111. Sustainable Fertilizer ProductionFertilizer production can be energy-intensive. Future approaches include green ammonia, renewable hydrogen, nutrient recycling, phosphorus recovery, biofertilizers, precision application, and low-carbon fertilizer manufacturing.112. Carbon FarmingCarbon farming aims to increase carbon storage in agricultural soils and vegetation. Methods include cover crops, reduced tillage, agroforestry, rotational grazing, biochar, soil restoration, and measurement of agricultural carbon credits.113. Greenhouse-Gas Emissions from AgricultureAgriculture produces methane, nitrous oxide, and carbon dioxide. Relevant areas include livestock methane, fertilizer emissions, rice cultivation, soil management, manure management, low-emission farming, methane-reducing feed, and carbon accounting.114. Methane Reduction in LivestockLivestock methane emissions can potentially be reduced through improved feed, feed additives, selective breeding, manure management, grazing practices, and monitoring technologies.115. Biochar in AgricultureBiochar is produced by heating organic material with limited oxygen and can be applied to soil. Potential areas include soil fertility, water retention, carbon storage, waste utilization, nutrient management, and restoration of degraded soils.116. Agricultural Carbon MarketsCarbon markets may provide farmers with financial incentives for reducing emissions or storing carbon. Relevant areas include carbon measurement, soil-carbon verification, carbon credits, remote monitoring, regenerative farming, and agricultural climate finance.117. Life-Cycle Assessment of FoodLife-cycle assessment measures environmental impacts across the entire food-production process. Areas include land use, water use, energy consumption, greenhouse-gas emissions, processing, packaging, transport, storage, and food waste.118. Sustainable Food ConsumptionConsumer choices influence agricultural production. Relevant areas include plant-rich diets, seasonal food, local sourcing, sustainable seafood, reduced food waste, environmental labelling, responsible purchasing, and dietary shifts.119. Digital Food LabelsDigital labels can provide consumers with more information about products. They may include QR codes showing origin, nutritional information, environmental footprint, farming practices, allergens, authenticity, and supply-chain history.120. Smart Food RetailTechnology can improve food availability and reduce retail waste. Areas include automated inventories, demand forecasting, smart shelves, dynamic pricing, expiry tracking, robotic warehouses, cashierless stores, and food-waste monitoring.121. Artificial Intelligence in Food Supply ChainsAI can improve forecasting and coordination across food systems. Applications include predicting demand, reducing excess inventory, optimizing transport, detecting quality problems, predicting food spoilage, managing warehouses, and identifying supply-chain risks.122. Predictive Analytics for Food SecurityPredictive analytics can combine weather, production, market, population, and satellite data to forecast food shortages. It can support early intervention, emergency planning, crop-yield estimation, price forecasting, and humanitarian assistance.123. Digital Twins in AgricultureDigital twins create virtual models of farms, greenhouses, machinery, animals, or agricultural systems. They can support simulation, predictive maintenance, crop-growth analysis, irrigation optimization, energy management, and testing of production strategies.124. Edge Computing in AgricultureEdge computing processes agricultural data close to where it is collected. This can support fast responses from drones, autonomous tractors, cameras, irrigation controllers, greenhouse systems, and livestock-monitoring devices without depending entirely on cloud connectivity.125. Cloud Computing in AgricultureCloud platforms allow agricultural data to be stored and analyzed remotely. Applications include farm-management platforms, satellite analysis, crop records, machine-learning models, supply-chain databases, equipment monitoring, and collaborative agricultural services.126. Autonomous AgricultureAutonomous farming combines robotics, AI, GPS, computer vision, and sensors to reduce direct human operation. Relevant areas include autonomous tractors, robotic seeding, automated spraying, robotic harvesting, driverless farm vehicles, and autonomous crop-monitoring systems.127. Computer Vision in AgricultureComputer vision allows machines to interpret agricultural images. Applications include weed detection, fruit counting, disease recognition, crop grading, livestock monitoring, robotic harvesting, plant-growth measurement, and food-quality inspection.128. Machine Learning for Crop PredictionMachine-learning models can analyze weather, soil, satellite, and farm data. Applications include yield prediction, disease forecasting, irrigation planning, fertilizer optimization, crop selection, and market forecasting.129. Smart Agricultural SensorsSensors are central to modern farming systems. Types include soil-moisture sensors, nutrient sensors, temperature sensors, humidity sensors, pH sensors, gas sensors, water-quality sensors, animal-health sensors, and optical crop sensors.130. RFID and Tracking SystemsRFID technology can identify and track livestock, food products, machinery, and agricultural inputs. It supports animal identification, warehouse management, supply-chain traceability, inventory control, and automated logistics.131. Agricultural Geographic Information SystemsGIS helps farmers and governments analyse spatial information. Applications include field mapping, soil mapping, irrigation planning, crop zoning, land-use analysis, drought maps, pest-distribution maps, and agricultural policy planning.132. Agricultural Decision-Support SystemsDecision-support systems combine data and models to help users choose appropriate actions. They can recommend irrigation schedules, fertilizer rates, planting dates, crop varieties, pest-control strategies, harvest timing, and responses to weather risks.133. Digital Crop ModelsCrop models simulate how plants develop under different conditions. They can examine temperature, rainfall, soil, irrigation, fertilizers, climate change, planting dates, and crop varieties to estimate production.134. Smart Greenhouses Powered by AIAI-controlled greenhouses can automatically manage temperature, humidity, light, irrigation, nutrients, ventilation, and energy consumption based on real-time sensor data and plant-growth models.135. Agricultural 3D Printing3D printing may be used to manufacture equipment parts, irrigation components, customized farm tools, food structures, laboratory equipment, and prototypes for agricultural machines.136. Agricultural NanobiosensorsAdvanced nanoscale sensors can potentially detect very small concentrations of pathogens, nutrients, toxins, pesticides, and plant-stress indicators, allowing earlier agricultural intervention.137. Synthetic Biology and FoodSynthetic biology can engineer microorganisms or cells to produce food ingredients, proteins, flavours, vitamins, and agricultural chemicals. Relevant areas include precision fermentation, engineered microbes, alternative proteins, and sustainable ingredient production.138. Precision FermentationPrecision fermentation uses microorganisms to manufacture specific food ingredients. Applications can include proteins, enzymes, fats, vitamins, dairy-like proteins, and food additives produced with reduced dependence on conventional livestock.139. Agricultural GenomicsGenomics studies the genetic information of crops and livestock. Applications include disease resistance, productivity improvement, heat tolerance, drought resistance, breeding programs, livestock genetics, and preservation of agricultural biodiversity.140. Gene Editing for Food SecurityGene-editing technologies can potentially develop crops that tolerate drought, heat, pests, diseases, and poor soils while improving yield and nutritional quality.141. Ethical Issues in Agricultural TechnologyAgricultural innovation raises questions concerning genetically modified organisms, data ownership, automation and employment, animal welfare, land concentration, access to technology, environmental risks, and control of agricultural genetic resources.142. Social Impacts of Agricultural AutomationAutomation can reduce physical labour but may also change rural employment. Relevant areas include job displacement, creation of skilled technical jobs, farmer training, rural inequality, migration, productivity, and technology access.143. Digital Divide in AgricultureNot every farmer has equal access to digital technology. Key issues include internet availability, device cost, digital literacy, farm size, electricity access, language barriers, training, and affordability of advanced machinery.144. Agricultural Policy and TechnologyGovernments influence agricultural innovation through subsidies, research programs, digital infrastructure, equipment grants, environmental regulations, food-safety laws, biotechnology rules, and agricultural education.145. Regulation of Agricultural BiotechnologyBiotechnology requires frameworks governing genetically modified crops, gene-edited plants, food safety, environmental risk, seed approval, labelling, intellectual property, and international trade.146. Regulation of Agricultural DronesDrone use in agriculture involves aviation rules, spraying permissions, operator licensing, data privacy, remote identification, restricted airspace, and environmental regulations.147. Standards for Smart AgricultureInteroperability becomes important as agricultural equipment becomes connected. Relevant areas include communication standards, sensor compatibility, machinery-data formats, cybersecurity standards, IoT protocols, and equipment certification.148. Intellectual Property in AgricultureAgricultural innovation involves patents, plant-variety protection, seed ownership, biotechnology patents, farm-software licences, indigenous knowledge, and access to genetic resources.149. Agricultural Cooperatives and TechnologyCooperatives can make expensive technology more accessible. Farmers can jointly purchase machinery, drones, storage facilities, processing equipment, digital services, irrigation infrastructure, and renewable-energy systems.150. Smart Agricultural CooperativesDigital platforms can improve cooperative management through shared machinery booking, digital payments, member records, market coordination, group purchasing, crop forecasting, logistics, and collective sales.151. Rural Agricultural InfrastructureFood security depends on infrastructure such as roads, electricity, irrigation canals, storage facilities, telecommunications, markets, laboratories, processing centres, and cold-storage networks.152. Agricultural Mechanization in Developing RegionsMechanization can increase productivity where agriculture depends heavily on manual labour. Important issues include affordable machinery, equipment sharing, local manufacturing, maintenance services, financing, training, and adaptation to small farms.153. Food Security in Developing CountriesMajor challenges include low agricultural productivity, climate vulnerability, poverty, conflict, poor infrastructure, limited irrigation, food losses, inadequate storage, market access, malnutrition, and technological gaps.154. Food Security in Arid RegionsDry regions require specialized approaches such as desalination, drip irrigation, greenhouse agriculture, drought-resistant crops, treated wastewater, hydroponics, water harvesting, soil-moisture conservation, and strategic food imports.155. Food Security in Island NationsIsland countries can face limited farmland, dependence on imports, transport costs, climate risks, and vulnerability to supply disruptions. Technologies such as vertical farming, hydroponics, aquaculture, renewable energy, and local food storage can improve resilience.156. Food Security in MegacitiesLarge cities require reliable food supply networks. Areas include urban agriculture, wholesale markets, transport logistics, cold storage, food reserves, vertical farming, food-waste reduction, last-mile delivery, and emergency food planning.157. Population Growth and Food DemandGrowing populations increase demand for crops, livestock products, water, land, and agricultural energy. Relevant areas include sustainable intensification, yield improvement, alternative proteins, food-loss reduction, efficient distribution, and changing diets.158. Sustainable IntensificationSustainable intensification seeks to produce more food from existing farmland while minimizing environmental impacts. It involves precision agriculture, improved seeds, irrigation efficiency, integrated pest management, soil conservation, and better nutrient management.159. Agricultural ProductivityProductivity can be improved through mechanization, better seeds, irrigation, fertilizers, precision agriculture, farmer training, research, improved infrastructure, digital technologies, and efficient supply chains.160. Resilient Cropping SystemsResilient crop systems can continue producing food despite climate or economic shocks. Important approaches include crop diversification, resilient seeds, irrigation, soil conservation, agroforestry, local seed systems, crop insurance, and digital early-warning systems.161. Crop DiversificationGrowing different crops can reduce dependence on a single crop and improve resilience. Relevant areas include intercropping, crop rotation, mixed farming, indigenous crops, climate-resilient crops, soil-health improvement, and market diversification.162. Indigenous Agricultural KnowledgeTraditional farming methods can contribute to sustainable food systems. Areas include local crop varieties, traditional irrigation, seed preservation, soil management, agroforestry, natural pest control, and adaptation to local climates.163. Seed Banks and Genetic ConservationSeed banks preserve crop genetic diversity for future breeding and food security. Important areas include long-term seed storage, genetic databases, rare crop varieties, wild crop relatives, community seed banks, and international genetic-resource conservation.164. Agricultural Biodiversity ConservationMaintaining a broad range of crops, livestock breeds, insects, and soil organisms can reduce vulnerability to diseases, environmental change, and market shocks.165. Food System ResilienceA resilient food system can adapt to environmental, economic, health, or political disruptions. It includes diversified production, local processing, strategic reserves, strong transport networks, multiple suppliers, digital monitoring, renewable energy, and emergency planning.166. Agricultural Resilience to PandemicsPandemics can disrupt farm labour, transportation, processing plants, markets, and international trade. Relevant responses include automation, local food production, contactless logistics, digital marketplaces, strategic reserves, and diversified supply chains.167. Food Security During Natural DisastersNatural disasters can interrupt production and distribution. Relevant areas include emergency food reserves, rapid agricultural assessment, mobile food-processing systems, satellite monitoring, emergency logistics, drought-resistant crops, and disaster-resilient storage.168. Humanitarian Food TechnologyTechnology can support food assistance through digital food vouchers, biometric distribution systems, mobile payments, nutrition monitoring, fortified emergency food, supply-chain tracking, and predictive hunger modelling.169. Agricultural Risk ManagementFarmers face weather, market, disease, financial, and operational risks. Relevant tools include insurance, diversification, forecasting, digital monitoring, crop storage, irrigation, financial planning, and disaster preparedness.170. Future of AgricultureFuture agriculture is likely to combine autonomous machinery, AI, robotics, biotechnology, vertical farming, precision agriculture, renewable energy, climate-smart systems, alternative proteins, digital supply chains, and increasingly data-driven management.171. Future of Food SecurityFuture food security will depend on whether societies can produce sufficient nutritious food while dealing with population growth, climate change, water scarcity, land degradation, conflicts, changing diets, resource limits, and supply-chain risks. Agricultural technology will play a central role through higher productivity, resilient crops, efficient resource use, better storage, intelligent distribution, and alternative food-production systems.

postings.conferenceText: 15th International Conference on Parallel, Distributed Computing Technologies and Applications (PDCTA 2026) November 21 ~ 22, 2026, London, United Kingdom https://soen2026.org/pdcta/index Scope 15th Conference on Parallel, Distributed Computing Technologies and Applications (PDCTA 2026) will provide an excellent international forum for sharing knowledge and results in theory, methodology and applications of Parallel, Distributed Computing. Original papers are invited on Algorithms and Applications, computer Networks, Cyber trust and security, Wireless networks and mobile computing and Bioinformatics. The aim of the conference is to provide a platform to the researchers and practitioners from both academia as well as industry to meet and share cutting-edge development in the field. to the researchers and practitioners from both academia as well as industry to meet and share cutting-edge development in the fieldAuthors are solicited to contribute to the conference by submitting articles that illustrate research results, projects, surveying works and industrial experiences that describe significant advances in the following areas, but are not limited to. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to, the following Parallel Algorithms Distributed Algorithms Theory of Parallel & Distributed Computing Task Based Parallelism Heterogeneous Computing Supercomputing & Exascale Systems Deterministic Distributed Systems Distributed Systems Geo Distributed Systems Planet Scale Databases Cloud Computing Multi Cloud & Hybrid Cloud Systems Edge & Fog postings.conferenceText: Call for papers/TopicsAll Abstracts, Reviews, short articles, Full articles, Posters are welcomed related with any of the following research fields:Foundational & Independent TopicsThese disciplines focus on specific lenses of human expression, communication, history, and behavior.1. LiteratureThe study of written, oral, and visual texts as artistic and cultural expressions. Literary Genres: Prose fiction, poetry, drama, creative nonfiction, and graphic narratives. Literary Periods and Movements: Classical, Medieval, Renaissance, Enlightenment, Romanticism, Realism, Modernism, and Postmodernism. Literary Theory and Criticism: Formalism, psychoanalytic criticism, Marxist theory, feminist theory, postcolonialism, and queer theory. Comparative Literature: Cross-cultural textual analysis, translation studies, and thematic transformations across geographies. 2. Linguistics and LanguagesThe scientific study of language structure, development, and use. Structural Linguistics: Phonetics (speech sounds), phonology (sound systems), morphology (word structure), syntax (sentence structure), and semantics (meaning). Historical Linguistics: Language evolution, language families, etymology, and language change over time. Sociolinguistics: Dialects, sociolects, language attitudes, code-switching, and the relationship between language and identity. Psycholinguistics and Neurolinguistics: Language acquisition (first and second language), sentence processing, and language localization in the brain. 3. HistoryThe study and interpretation of the human past through primary and secondary sources. Chronological and Regional History: Ancient, medieval, early modern, and contemporary history across global regions. Historiography: The philosophy and methodology of historical writing and how historical interpretations change. Social and Cultural History: The daily lives of ordinary people, gender roles, popular culture, and history from below. Political and Diplomatic History: The evolution of states, empires, international treaties, warfare, and governance. 4. PhilosophyThe critical investigation of fundamental questions regarding existence, knowledge, values, and reason. Epistemology: The nature, scope, and limits of knowledge and belief. Metaphysics: The nature of reality, existence, time, mind, and matter. Ethics and Moral Philosophy: Normative ethics, meta-ethics, and applied ethics (e.g., bioethics, environmental ethics). Logic: The principles of valid reasoning, formal logic, and informal fallacies. Interrelated & Social Science TopicsThese fields naturally blend humanistic inquiry with empirical, behavioral, and structural social sciences.1. Anthropology and ArchaeologyThe study of human beings, their ancestors, and cultures across time and space. Cultural Anthropology: Ethnography, kinship systems, rituals, belief systems, and globalization. Linguistic Anthropology: How language shapes social life, identity, and cultural worldview. Biological Anthropology: Human evolution, primatology, and forensic anthropology. Archaeology: Material culture analysis, excavation methodologies, and the preservation of cultural heritage. 2. Sociology and Social TheoryThe study of society, social institutions, social patterns, and human social behavior. Social Stratification and Inequality: Class dynamics, systemic racism, gender disparities, and social mobility. Sociology of Institutions: The study of family structures, education systems, religious organizations, and the state. Urban and Rural Sociology: Community development, urbanization, gentrification, and spatial inequalities. Demography: Population trends, migration patterns, aging, and birth/mortality rates. 3. Political Science and International RelationsThe study of power, governance, political behavior, and global systems. Political Theory: Philosophical inquiries into justice, liberty, authority, and democracy. Comparative Politics: Analyzing and comparing domestic political systems, constitutions, and electoral mechanisms across countries. International Relations: Geopolitics, foreign policy, international law, and global organizations (e.g., the UN). Public Policy and Administration: Bureaucratic management, policy formulation, and the execution of state programs. 4. Psychology and Behavioral SciencesThe scientific study of the human mind and behavior. Cognitive Psychology: Memory, attention, perception, problem-solving, and decision-making. Social Psychology: Group dynamics, prejudice, conformity, interpersonal relationships, and social cognition. Developmental Psychology: Psychological shifts across the lifespan, from infancy to old age. Abnormal and Clinical Psychology: Mental health disorders, therapeutic frameworks, and psychiatric diagnoses. 5. Media, Communication, and Cultural StudiesThe intersection of technology, human interaction, and cultural production. Mass Communication: Journalism, broadcasting, media ethics, and the history of print and digital media. Digital Media and Technology Studies: Social media algorithms, digital cultures, virtual identity, and human-computer interaction. Cultural Studies: The analysis of power dynamics within popular culture, consumerism, mass media, and subcultures. Rhetoric and Public Discourse: The art of persuasion, political rhetoric, and communication theory

postings.conferenceName: LISBON 11th International Conference on Civil, Transportation & Environmental Engineering (LCTE2-27) scheduled on Feb. 3-5, 2027 Lisbon (Portugal)
postings.conferenceText: Call for papers/TopicsTopics of interest for submission include any topics related to:1. Civil Engineering Civil engineering provides the physical framework for both transportation systems and environmental infrastructure. Structural Engineering Design and analysis of bridges, buildings, and dams (interfaces with Transportation for bridge design). Structural dynamics and earthquake/seismic engineering. Material science (advanced concrete, steel, composites). Geotechnical Engineering Soil mechanics and rock mechanics. Foundation engineering (shallow and deep foundations for buildings and highways). Slope stability, retaining walls, and tunneling (critical for highway and transit routes). Construction Engineering & Management Project scheduling, costing, and BIM (Building Information Modeling). Sustainable construction practices and lifecycle asset management. 2. Transportation Engineering Transportation engineering relies heavily on civil engineering for physical assets and increasingly intersects with environmental engineering regarding emissions and urban planning. Traffic Engineering & Operations Traffic flow theory and capacity analysis. Signal optimization and Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS). Geometric design of highways and intersections. Transportation Planning & Policy Travel demand forecasting (the traditional 4-step model). Transit-oriented development (TOD) and multi-modal urban planning. Freight logistics and supply chain infrastructure. Pavement & Materials Engineering Asphalt and concrete pavement design (flexible and rigid). Pavement management systems and non-destructive testing. 3. Environmental Engineering Environmental engineering manages the impact of human activity on the planet, heavily interacting with civil infrastructure for water systems and transportation for air/noise pollution. Water Resources & Hydraulic Engineering Fluid mechanics and open channel flow. Hydrology (precipitation, runoff, flood routing). Stormwater management and sustainable urban drainage systems (SUDS). Water & Wastewater Treatment Physical, chemical, and biological treatment processes. Drinking water distribution network design. Industrial waste management and water reuse technologies. Air Quality & Noise Pollution Atmospheric dispersion modeling of vehicle emissions. Indoor air quality and greenhouse gas mitigation. Traffic noise assessment and barrier design. Solid & Hazardous Waste Management Landfill design and leachate management. Site remediation and brownfield redevelopment. 4. Interrelated & Overlapping DomainsThese subtopics sit at the direct intersection of two or all three disciplines, requiring a multidisciplinary approach. Sustainable Infrastructure & Resilient Cities (Civil + Transportation + Environmental) Evaluating the carbon footprint of mega-projects. Climate change adaptation for coastal roads, bridges, and drainage systems. Green infrastructure integration (e.g., permeable pavements for traffic that also manage stormwater). Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) (Transportation + Environmental) Assessing how new transit corridors or airports affect local ecosystems, air quality, and noise levels. Smart Cities & Urban Systems (Civil + Transportation) Autonomous vehicle infrastructure integration. Sensor networks for structural health monitoring of bridges and roads. Hydro-Fracturing & Geo-Environmental Engineering (Civil + Environmental) Contaminant transport through soil and groundwater. Designing secure containment barriers for hazardous waste landfills.

postings.conferenceName: BUDAPEST 7th International Congress on Artificial Intelligence: Challenges & Impacts (AICI-27)
postings.conferenceText: Call for papers/TopicsFull Articles/ Reviews/ Shorts Papers/ Abstracts are welcomed in the following research fields:Foundational & Independent ChallengesThese areas focus on the distinct technical, ethical, and immediate operational bottlenecks inherent to the development and deployment of AI systems.1. Technical Risks and Algorithmic VulnerabilitiesThe inherent failures and security gaps built directly into AI architectures and data pipelines. The "Black Box" Problem: Lack of interpretability and explainability in deep neural networks. Hallucination and Error Propagation: The tendency of large models to confidently generate false, unverified information. Adversarial Exploitation: Vulnerabilities to prompt injection, data poisoning, and model inversion attacks. Data Quality and Scarcity: Managing biased, missing, or unrepresentative datasets that degrade model accuracy. 2. Ethical and Algorithmic GovernanceThe fundamental human rights, fairness, and accountability dilemmas posed by autonomous code. Algorithmic Bias and Discrimination: Implicit and explicit biases in training data leading to discriminatory outcomes in hiring, lending, or law enforcement. Plagiarism and Intellectual Property: Unauthorized scraping of copyrighted data to train proprietary foundation models. Autonomous Agency and Legal Liability: Determining accountability (developer vs. user vs. manufacturer) when an autonomous system causes physical or financial harm. Privacy and Surveillance Overreach: Infringement of individual data rights via mass biometric tracking and non-consensual personal profiling. 3. Resource and Environmental SustainabilityThe physical constraints and material footprint required to power digital intelligence. Energy Demand and Carbon Footprint: Extreme power consumption of hyperscale data centers needed for training and inference. Water Consumption: High volumes of fresh water required to cool high-performance AI compute hardware. Electronic Waste (E-Waste): Rapid hardware obsolescence cycles for advanced processing units (GPUs and TPUs). Interrelated & Systemic ImpactsThese fields represent the massive, overlapping consequences where AI intersects with economics, society, information ecosystems, and global security.1. Labor Markets and Economic StratificationThe disruptive convergence of corporate automation, changing skill requirements, and wealth distribution. Job Displacement vs. Augmentation: The replacement of routine cognitive and manual labor versus the creation of human-in-the-loop hybrid roles. The AI Divide: Widening economic inequalities between tech-monopoly nations and developing economies with weak digital infrastructure. Skill Devaluation and Cognitive Dependence: The atrophy of human critical thinking and technical skills due to over-reliance on automated tools. 2. Information Integrity and Societal CohesionThe space where advanced generative capabilities reshape human communication, trust, and psychological safety. Synthetic Media and Deepfakes: The proliferation of ultra-realistic audio and video used for targeted defamation, fraud, and political subversion. Algorithmic Echo Chambers: Recommendation engines optimized for engagement that accidentally accelerate radicalization and public polarization. Mass-Produced Disinformation: The low-cost scaling of persuasive, fabricated news designed to destabilize public trust in democratic systems. 3. Geopolitics, Warfare, and Global SecurityThe intersection of state power, defense strategy, and the race for technological supremacy. Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS): Drones and robotic systems authorized to select and engage targets without direct human intervention. The AGI Hegemony Race: Geopolitical competition between major global powers to achieve Artificial General Intelligence first, upsetting the balance of power. Asymmetric Cyber Warfare: Automated vulnerability discovery and AI-driven social engineering attacks launched by state-sponsored actors. 4. Sociotechnical Transformation of Public SectorsHow the structural integration of AI alters the fundamental delivery of healthcare, education, and justice. Automated Judicial Bias: Risk of systemic bias in predictive sentencing software and automated risk assessments. Diagnostic and Clinical Over-reliance: Medical errors resulting from physicians relying too heavily on algorithmic triage and diagnostic software. Plagiarism and Educational Redesign: The breakdown of traditional assessment methods in academia, forcing a total overhaul of pedagogy and grading

postings.conferenceText: Call for papers/Topics All Abstracts, Reviews, short articles, Full articles, Posters are welcomed related with any of the following research fields:1. Medical Sciences (Human Medicine)Medical sciences focus primarily on the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of human disease, heavily anchored in advanced pathology and clinical interventions.Independent Medical Topics Pathology and Pathophysiology: Cellular adaptations, tissue inflammation, mechanisms of neoplasia (tumor growth), and systemic organ failure. Clinical Pharmacology: Therapeutics, pharmacokinetics (how the body processes drugs), drug-drug interactions, and toxicodynamics. Medical Diagnostics and Imaging: Radiology (X-ray, MRI, CT scans), molecular diagnostics, histopathology, and laboratory medicine. Surgical Specialties: General surgery, orthopedic surgery, neurosurgery, cardiothoracic interventions, and minimally invasive procedures. Internal Medicine Subspecialties: Cardiology, gastroenterology, neurology, endocrinology, nephrology, and pulmonology. Interrelated Medical Subtopics Neuro-Medicine: The overlap between neurology (physical brain structures) and psychiatry (mental health conditions). Cardio-Pulmonary Medicine: The tight interaction between heart function and respiratory health during acute diseases. 2. Nursing SciencesNursing centers on holistic patient care, health promotion, clinical management, and the human response to acute and chronic illnesses.Independent Nursing Topics Fundamentals of Nursing: Patient assessment, vital signs monitoring, hygiene care, wound management, and basic clinical procedures. Nursing Theories and Frameworks: Orem’s self-care deficit theory, Watson’s theory of human caring, and the nursing process (Assessment, Diagnosis, Planning, Implementation, Evaluation). Community and Public Health Nursing: Home health care, epidemiology in communities, outbreak containment, and preventative health education. Nursing Leadership and Management: Ward management, healthcare resource allocation, staffing models, and clinical auditing. Advanced Practice Nursing: Clinical nurse specialists, nurse anesthetists, and nurse practitioners. Interrelated Nursing Subtopics Psychiatric-Mental Health Nursing: Intersecting nursing care models with clinical psychiatry to manage complex mental health crises. Maternal-Child Nursing: Combining obstetrics, neonatology, and pediatrics into a continuous care model for mothers and infants. 3. Veterinary SciencesVeterinary sciences explore the health, behavior, and medical treatment of non-human animals, spanning companion animals, livestock, and wildlife.Independent Veterinary Topics Comparative Animal Anatomy and Physiology: Structural and functional differences between monogastric animals (dogs, pigs) and ruminants (cattle, sheep). Production Animal Medicine (Livestock): Herd health management, dairy and meat production optimization, and poultry medicine. Companion Animal Medicine: Canine, feline, and equine internal medicine, surgery, and preventative wellness. Exotic and Wildlife Medicine: Avian medicine, reptile therapeutics, zoo animal management, and conservation medicine. Veterinary Theriogenology: Animal reproduction, artificial insemination, embryotransfer, and obstetrics. Interrelated Veterinary Subtopics Equine Sports Medicine: Blending musculoskeletal physiology, biomechanics, and targeted physical therapy for performance horses. Veterinary Behavioral Medicine: The intersection of animal psychology, neurobiology, and environmental management to treat behavioral issues. 4. Interrelated Fields (The Convergence Zones)These critical topics sit directly at the intersection of Nursing, Medical, and Veterinary Sciences, showcasing how the fields rely on one another.One Health (The Medical-Veterinary-Environmental Interface) Zoonotic Diseases: Pathogens that leap between animals and humans, such as rabies, avian influenza, and brucellosis. Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR): How antibiotic overuse in both livestock farming (Veterinary) and human clinics (Medical) drives global bacterial resistance. Comparative Medicine: Studying naturally occurring diseases in animals (like cancers in dogs) to better understand and cure similar diseases in humans. Food Safety and Security: Veterinary inspection of animal products ensuring toxicological and microbiological safety before human consumption. Clinical Teamwork and Systems Interface Interprofessional Collaboration: How nurses and physicians coordinate in high-stress clinical environments to reduce medical errors. Translational Research: Applying laboratory discoveries in basic medical and veterinary sciences directly into bedside nursing and clinical treatments. Bioethics and Medical Law: Navigating end-of-life care, informed consent, and animal welfare regulations across clinical practices
